title: We Already Ran the Experiment
author: Caleb Collier
summary: Caleb Collier, writing as a guest post on Restarting School, revisits the Eight-Year Study (1930-1942), in which 280 American colleges agreed to waive standard admissions requirements for graduates of 29 experimental high schools that redesigned their curricula around integrated, problem-based, student-driven learning instead of the credit-counting Carnegie unit. Ralph Tyler's rigorous matched-pair evaluation found experimental-school graduates modestly outperformed traditional-school peers overall on both academic and character measures -- and that the six schools that departed most radically from convention outperformed by the widest margins, while the two least-changed schools showed no advantage at all, suggesting more innovation produced more benefit, not less safety. Collier's real argument, though, is about why the reform vanished within a decade despite the positive results: it launched with weak public buy-in, never brought parents and communities into the design process, and lost its support infrastructure once the world war ended attention and funding. He closes with a sharper irony -- Tyler's own evaluation method, designed to give unconventional schools a fair hearing, was later adapted into the standards-based accountability regime that now constrains the very kind of experimentation it was built to protect.
points: In the Eight-Year Study's matched-pair evaluation, the six experimental schools that departed most radically from conventional curricula outperformed their traditional-school counterparts by the widest margins, while the two schools that changed the least showed no advantage at all -- evidence that more innovation, not moderate compromise, drove the gains.

More than 280 colleges agreed to waive standard admissions requirements -- required credits, prescribed subjects, entrance exams -- for graduates of the 29 participating high schools, trusting the principal's word instead, a scale of institutional buy-in modern reform efforts rarely attempt.

Collier argues the reform collapsed within a decade after its 1942 report not for lack of evidence but because it was imposed on communities rather than built with them, leaving no local constituency to defend it once wartime attention and funding moved on.

In a final irony, Ralph Tyler's own evaluation method -- built specifically to give unconventional schools a fair hearing since existing tests couldn't measure what they were doing -- was later generalized into the standards-based accountability framework that now enforces the rigid, test-driven model the Eight-Year Study was designed to escape.
quotes: For eight years, they asked, would you admit students from thirty specific high schools without any of your normal requirements? No required credits. No prescribed subjects. No entrance examinations. Just the principal's word that the student was ready. More than 280 colleges said yes.

Nobody designed the Carnegie unit as a theory of learning. It was a bookkeeping convention. But by 1930 it functioned as a theory of learning anyway, and the theory it encoded was this: time in a seat equals knowledge acquired.

It wasn't that a moderate amount of innovation was safe. It was that the further a school went, the better its students did. That is not what a cautious person would predict, and it is not what the incremental, split-the-difference version of school reform assumes.

The final report came out in 1942, in five volumes, under the series title Adventure in American Education. It landed a few months after Pearl Harbor. Within about a decade, nearly every school in the study had gone back to the way it was before.

That approach, the practice of stating your objectives and then measuring against them, became the foundation of modern educational assessment and eventually of standards-based accountability. The tool invented to protect an experiment in freedom outlived the experiment and was turned around to enforce the thing it was built to escape.

The most radical act of the Eight-Year Study wasn't redesigning a curriculum. It was persuading 280 institutions to let go of the gate for eight years and see what came through. What came through was good. We've known that since 1942.
